older adults who have fallen recently have greater variability in their sustained attention compared to older adults who have not fallen.
greater variability in sustained attention, measured by the SART, is a retrospective predictor of falls in older adults and is weakly correlated with falls efficacy.
older adults who have more falls have greater variability in sustained attention and that variability in sustained attention may be a biomarker for falls.

the development of a new and innovative method for assessing sustained attention in older people and its relationship to falls and falls efficacy.
the relationship between attention and falls in older adults and the implications of this for falls prevention.
the relationship between cognitive function and falls.

greater variability in sustained attention, particularly that associated with the top-down (vigilance) aspect of the task, may be a novel biomarker for falls and reduced falls efficacy in older people.
greater variability in sustained attention (particularly that associated with the arousal aspect of attention) is associated with falls in older adults.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the variability in the vigilance (i.e. top down) aspect of sustained visual attention is a strong predictor of falls.
older people who are less able to sustain their attention over time have greater difficulty with gait control and are more likely to experience a fall.
older adults who fall have greater variability in their attentional resources, and that this variability is associated with reduced falls efficacy, which in turn is a strong predictor of falls.

variability in the top-down (vigilance) aspects of sustained attention is associated both with falling and falls efficacy, and may be used as a retrospective biomarker for falls.
